A0038.title: Proxy Detection
A0038.definition: Detecting the use of proxies when users request network resources.
A0038.description: Proxy detection primarily analyzes the data characteristics of user requests to identify and assess the use of network proxies and terminal proxies, further confirming whether the request is from a real user.
A0038.limitation: The biggest problem with proxy detection is that normal users may also use proxies, making false positives easy.

A0038-001.title: Web Access Proxy Detection
A0038-001.definition: Detecting the access proxy used when users request resources (a typical access proxy is a web browser).
A0038-001.description: Black-gray industry actors may use non-standard web access proxies to request resources, such as headless browsers, curl, wget, or HTTP libraries from various programming languages. Detection methods include: User-Agent analysis, JavaScript environment detection, JA3 fingerprinting, HTTP/2 fingerprinting, etc.
A0038-001.limitation: Because web access proxy detection ultimately relies on analyzing terminal request information, placing this measure in a high-adversarial context makes it easy to bypass by forging and modifying data.

A0038-002.title: Network Proxy Detection
A0038-002.definition: Detecting whether users are using a network proxy when requesting resources.
A0038-002.description: Common network proxy methods include VPN, SOCKS5, and HTTP proxies. Current common network proxy detection methods include: IP intelligence, request IP clustering, IP attribute analysis, TCP/IP fingerprinting, DNS server location discrepancy, using WebRTC to expose the real IP, and leveraging the network latency characteristics of proxies to determine whether a network proxy is being used.
A0038-002.limitation: Network proxy detection has the following limitations: first, normal users may also use network proxies, making false positives easy; second, using mobile carrier egress IPs as proxies makes blocking difficult even when detected; third, using ADSL dial-up networks as proxies allows immediate switching to a new proxy by re-dialing after being blocked.

A0038-003.title: TLS/HTTP Fingerprinting
A0038-003.definition: Identifying the true client type via TLS handshake and HTTP/2 protocol-layer fingerprints, distinguishing real browsers from protocol crawlers and automation scripts.
A0038-003.description: TLS/HTTP fingerprinting is a technique that identifies client types based on protocol-layer characteristics. Typical fingerprints include: JA3/JA4 fingerprints (hashes computed from the TLS ClientHello's version, cipher suites, extensions, and elliptic curves, identifying the client's TLS implementation library such as OpenSSL, BoringSSL, or a browser TLS stack), HTTP/2 fingerprints (based on SETTINGS frame parameters, window updates, and header-compression dynamic tables, distinguishing browsers from curl/Python requests and similar libraries), and TCP/IP fingerprints (based on MSS, window size, and TCP options to distinguish operating systems). Real browsers and protocol crawlers or automation libraries have inherent differences in protocol-layer implementations — even if an attacker spoofs the User-Agent, the TLS/HTTP2 fingerprint still exposes the true client type. This measure is a protocol-layer supplement to the UA and JS-environment checks in web access proxy detection (A0038-001), harder to forge than UA, and an important technique for identifying protocol crawlers and automation scripts. Note the distinction from A0038-001: A0038-001 focuses on browser-proxy type identification (headless browsers, curl, wget, etc.), while A0038-003 focuses on the specific technique of underlying protocol fingerprinting.
A0038-003.limitation: Mainstream browser and automation-tool TLS fingerprints can be deliberately aligned (e.g., using curl-impersonate or modifying TLS library parameters to mimic browser fingerprints). JA3/JA4 fingerprint databases require continuous maintenance to cover new client versions. Some clients' fingerprints change with system/library upgrades, risking false positives. Intermediate layers such as CDNs and security gateways may rewrite TLS fingerprints and distort detection.
